We learned yesterday that a judge ruled that a lawsuit accusing Apple of violating state privacy laws with the face recognition feature in the Photos app can proceed, involving $32 billion in damages.

Although the two companies are at opposite ends of the privacy spectrum, this case has been conflated with one related to Meta's use of face recognition, and the court essentially failed to understand how this feature works when allowing the case to proceed...

Earlier allegations against Meta

To properly understand the current situation, we need to start with a lawsuit that can be traced back to 2015.

Since face recognition was performed on Meta's servers, and Meta was able to identify these people's identities, the company did indeed break the law and ultimately had to settle with the plaintiffs, paying $650 million.

Apple is now being sued under the same Illinois law — the Biometric Information Privacy Act (BIPA) — which prohibits companies from collecting biometric data without consent.

Apple's approach is completely different

There is a major problem with this allegation: when Apple performs face recognition in the Photos app, it does not collect any biometric data at all. As Apple pointed out in a machine learning research paper published in 2021, the recognition algorithm runs entirely on the device locally.

Furthermore, the iPhone only identifies that "the people in these photos look like they might be the same person" — it has no idea who that person actually is. Only the iPhone user themselves can name them.

Apple's Photos app privacy policy also reflects this point.

This lawsuit has been纠缠 in the court system for six years. I am just shocked that these allegations — which could be easily debunked with just a few minutes of verification — have been allowed to proceed.

The courts and legislators should actively support privacy-protecting approaches like Apple's, rather than lumping them together with privacy-invading behaviour from companies like Meta.

This is another example of courts and legislators fundamentally not understanding the technology they are trying to regulate. The most obvious example is, of course, end-to-end encryption. Multiple countries have threatened or even attempted to ban end-to-end encryption, despite the fact that they don't understand how it works at all.

Of course, I understand that judges and politicians cannot be expected to know everything. But they can invite experts to provide advice, and what I find hard to believe is that some lawsuits and legislative attempts that have made such obvious fundamental errors have been able to纠缠 for years without anyone pointing out the problems.
